issues.legal_issue: An employee’s suspension pending disciplinary proceedings cannot be continued indefinitely before formal charges are served, and any extension after service of charges requires a reasoned order.
material_facts: The employee had remained continuously suspended for several years while criminal investigation delayed the commencement of departmental proceedings.
Formal charges had not been served during the prolonged suspension, although the suspension had been repeatedly renewed and reasons had been recorded for the renewals.
The government said departmental proceedings could not commence while the criminal investigation was pending.
By the time the Court disposed of the appeal, a chargesheet had been served on the employee.
issues.conclusion: A suspension pending disciplinary proceedings should not extend beyond three months if a memorandum of charges or chargesheet has not been served within that period. If charges have been served, any extension of suspension must be supported by a reasoned order. The Court also held that the employee, whose chargesheet had by then been served, could challenge continued suspension through available legal means, subject to judicial review.
issues.legal_principle: Article 21 protects the right to a speedy trial, and that right encompasses the stages of investigation, inquiry and trial; expedition and diligence are also expected in departmental inquiries. The Court drew on the proviso to Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which limits pre-trial detention, and applied its underlying concern for liberty and human dignity by analogy to suspension. It relied on Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab and Raghubir Singh v. State of Bihar in discussing the statutory and constitutional context, and on Abdul Rehman Antulay v. R.S. Nayak for the scope of the speedy-trial right and the need to assess delay in context. It also referred to O.P. Gupta v. Union of India on the harm of prolonged suspension, K. Sukhendar Reddy v. State of A.P. on indefinite selective suspension, and State of A.P. v. N. Radhakishan on prejudice from unexplained delay. The Court considered, but distinguished on the facts, Union of India v. Dipak Mali and Ravi Yashwant Bhoir v. District Collector, Raigad.

predicates.departmental_inquiry_suspension: An employee was suspended pending a departmental or disciplinary inquiry.
predicates.charges_not_served_within_initial_window: The employee was not served with formal charges within the initial period of suspension contemplated by the rule.
predicates.suspension_extension_sought: The employer sought to continue the employee’s suspension beyond its existing period.
predicates.continued_suspension_requires_timely_cha: The suspension cannot continue without timely service of formal charges, and any extension after charges are served must be supported by a reasoned order.

issues.definition: When an employee is suspended pending a departmental inquiry, continued suspension requires timely service of formal charges, and an extension after their service must be supported by a reasoned order.
